title: Wieland–Miescher ketone 1: Michael addition
subtitle: A 1,3-dione adds to methyl vinyl ketone

reactants.caption: 2-methylcyclohexane-1,3-dione + methyl vinyl ketone + potassium hydroxide
reactants.learnerPrompt: Hydroxide makes the nucleophile. Which proton does it take?
hintTiers: The hydrogen between the two ring C=O groups is unusually acidic (pKa about 5): its anion is shared by both oxygens.
Hydroxide takes the drawn hydrogen on the ring carbon carrying the methyl group. The C–H pair forms a C=C bond to one carbonyl carbon, and that C=O π pair moves onto oxygen. Three arrows.
Hydroxide lone pair → new bond to the drawn hydrogen; that C–H bond → a π bond to a ring carbonyl carbon; that C=O π bond → a lone pair on its oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Hydroxide adding to a ketone is reversible and leads nowhere here. The dione has a very acidic C–H: take that proton.
Hydroxide could add to the enone, but the far more acidic dione is deprotonated first. Make the dione enolate.
The methyl hydrogens of methyl vinyl ketone (pKa about 20) are far less acidic than the C–H between two C=O groups (pKa about 5).

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Good: hydroxide takes the proton and a C=C bond forms. Now move the C=O π pair onto oxygen.

enolate.caption: the dione enolate + methyl vinyl ketone + water
enolate.learnerPrompt: The enolate adds to methyl vinyl ketone (Michael addition).
hintTiers: Methyl vinyl ketone has two electrophilic carbons. A soft, stabilised enolate adds to the far end of the C=C.
The O⁻ lone pair re-forms C=O, the enolate C=C pair makes a new bond to the CH₂ end of the alkene, the alkene π pair moves towards the carbonyl, and the C=O π pair goes onto oxygen. Four arrows.

Enolate O⁻ lone pair → C=O π bond; enolate C=C π bond → new bond to the CH₂ end of the enone; enone C=C π bond → a π bond between the middle carbon and the carbonyl carbon; enone C=O π bond → a lone pair on its oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Attack through oxygen gives an enol ether that falls apart again. The productive C–C bond comes from the enolate carbon.
Adding to the carbonyl carbon (1,2-addition) is reversible for a stabilised enolate. The far end of the C=C is the soft electrophile: conjugate addition.
The middle alkene carbon is not electrophilic. The positive end of the enone is the CH₂ carbon, two atoms from the C=O.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right bonds, but the ring carbonyl carbon is left short of electrons. Push the O⁻ lone pair in to re-form its C=O.

new-enolate.caption: the new enolate + water
hintTiers: The new enolate is much more basic than the dione enolate. Water can protonate it.
Protonate on carbon to give the ketone: the O⁻ lone pair re-forms C=O, the C=C pair takes the drawn hydrogen of water, and the O–H pair stays on water's oxygen. Three arrows.
Enolate O⁻ lone pair → C=O π bond; C=C π bond → new bond from the carbon next to the CH₂ to the drawn hydrogen of water; water's O–H bond → a lone pair on its oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Breaking the new C–C bond just reverses the Michael addition. Protonate the enolate.
Protonating oxygen gives the enol, which then tautomerises. Protonate carbon to reach the ketone directly.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right bonds, but this leaves a positive carbon next to O⁻. Push the O⁻ lone pair in to re-form C=O.

steps.explanationAfterStep: The anion of a 1,3-dione is shared by two oxygens, so only a catalytic amount of hydroxide is needed and the dione stays deprotonated in preference to everything else in the flask.
Conjugate addition builds the quaternary carbon: it now carries the methyl group, both ring carbonyls and the new side chain. The charge moves onto the enone's oxygen.
The ketone enolate (pKa about 20) is far more basic than the dione anion, so water protonates it and hydroxide is returned: the base is a catalyst.

mechanismSummary: Hydroxide removes the very acidic C–H between the two carbonyl groups of 2-methylcyclohexane-1,3-dione. The delocalised enolate adds to the far end of methyl vinyl ketone, building a quaternary carbon, and water protonates the new enolate on carbon, returning hydroxide. The product, 2-methyl-2-(3-oxobutyl)cyclohexane-1,3-dione, is the triketone that closes the second ring. Its two ring carbonyls are mirror images of each other: which one is attacked next decides the hand of the product.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 26 (conjugate addition, Robinson annulation)
Wieland and Miescher, Helvetica Chimica Acta 1950, 33, 2215
Ramachandran and Newman, Organic Syntheses 1961, 41, 38 (the triketone and the racemic ketone)
